children: It's no surprise that after building a business selling wood flooring, Lumber Liquidators founder Tom Sullivan filled his roughly 122.5-acre Tennessee ranch with an array of unusual wooden pieces: olive flooring and handrails, a cherry-blossom chandelier, and wall coverings made from scraps of reclaimed lumber.

Now looking to downsize, Tom is listing the property, located about 25 miles from Nashville in the village of Leiper's Fork, for $34.8 million. If it sells for close to that amount, it would be a record for the village, said listing agent Jamie Parsons of Compass.
Tom, 67, is a former contractor who founded Lumber Liquidators in 1993. The company went public in 2007. Tom bought it back in 2024 after the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
Tom and his wife, Britta Sullivan, paid $3.1 million in 2019 for the ranch, property records show.

The Sullivans, who also have homes in Miami Beach, Fla., Cohasset, Mass., New York City and Bordeaux, France, began looking more than a decade ago for property near the Lumber Liquidators' headquarters and distribution center  in Tennessee, Tom said.
The Sullivans lived in an older home on the Leiper's Fork property for a few years while designing a new, roughly 13,680-square-foot, six-bedroom house, as well as multiple barns and outbuildings.

Tom said it took two years just to get a permit for a new stone bridge over a creek — which visitors cross to reach the main residence — during which time the project grew. "It started off as a little stone house," he said of the initial plan. "It got bigger and bigger."

Throughout the home, Tom gravitated toward vibrant colors and bold patterns. "People usually see the wallpaper and go, 'What the hell is this?' " he said. The house has a 16-foot custom brass bar, and the study has leather flooring, with custom wood walls.

Construction took several years, and was completed the day before Thanksgiving last year, when the Sullivans hosted 16 guests. "We were barely moved in," he said. Tom and Britta have two young children; Tom has two older kids from a previous relationship.
Asked how much he invested, Tom said, "I'm afraid to add it up, but a lot." The road and bridge alone cost more than $6 million, he added.

Tom began thinking of selling the house this summer after Bed, Bath & Beyond signed a letter of intent to buy Lumber Liquidators. The deal fell through in September, but Tom said they no longer need such a large house. He plans to build a smaller home on a piece of adjacent land. He also has land in Vermont and Massachusetts where he would like to build.

Leiper's Fork is a tight-knit community where prices have shot up over the past few years, said Parsons. She cited a home in the area that sold for $6.25 million in 2020, then resold for $10.5 million in 2024. A roughly 208-acre property nearby sold for $19 million in January.
